Here, VillageReach takes over our account with #SocialWithSabin as part of #CervicalCancerAwarenessMonth, sharing a success story from #Nigeria ⤵️  --  Enugu has stood out as a top performer among all South-Eastern Nigerian states in driving HPV vaccine uptake, with 99% coverage as of October 2025, and our partners at the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) have recognized the progress there, especially around key efforts like Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (MNCH) Weeks.  🔥 How we did it:  Townhall-style dialogues brought people together — moms, teachers, chiefs, religious leaders, and young people — to talk honestly about HPV and the vaccine, where questions were welcomed and fears were respectfully unpacked through:  ✨ Trust: Health workers broke down the science, teachers explained school delivery logistics, and local leaders tied health protection to family and faith. ✨ Action: Caregivers and adolescents who wanted the adolescent to receive the vaccine were linked to on-site vaccination teams. ✨ Partnership: Together with the NPHCDA and local health agencies, Enugu communities kept HPV vaccination visible and accessible, with state leadership setting the direction. We supported school-based delivery and church-based sensitization to build comfort and confidence about the HPV vaccine among girls and those around them. post_message: In #Cameroon’s Nylon Health District, low #HPV vaccination rates posed a significant risk, especially given the high burden of cervical and other HPV-related cancers.   Routine immunization services were limited in reach, missed opportunities for vaccination were common, and low awareness and mistrust among some parents and health workers posed additional barriers.   To tackle these challenges, Nylon Health District launched a catalytic program — supported by Sabin and the World Health Organization — to improve HPV vaccination coverage by engaging schools, communities, and health facilities.   The results? 2,681 adolescents — 2.6 times the target — received the vaccine. Dive into Jeanne Liliane Mbengue’s case study on how the team achieved this milestone ⤵   https://bit.ly/3YNfw6n

post_message: The Sabin Vaccine Institute announced it has completed enrollment in all six Phase 2 clinical trials for its cAd3-Marburg Vaccine and its cAd3-Sudan Ebolavirus Vaccine candidates.  There are no licensed vaccines for protection against disease caused by Marburg virus or the Sudan virus strain of Ebola. Both are highly contagious hemorrhagic fever diseases that can have a high fatality rate of up to 88%.    Phase 2 clinical trials to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of the two monovalent vaccines, both on the cAd3 platform, began in healthy volunteers in Africa in 2023 and in the United States in 2025. The African trials, with sites in Kenya and Uganda, completed participant follow-up last year and reporting activities are progressing. The U.S. trials completed enrollment last month.  In addition, Sabin’s cAd3-Marburg Vaccine has been used in Phase 2 rapid response outbreak clinical trials in Africa — more than 1,700 participants enrolled in 2024 during an outbreak in Rwanda, and more than 500 participants enrolled beginning last December for Ethiopia’s first-ever Marburg outbreak.   Learn more ⤵️  https://ow.ly/K19e50YrNbg

post_message: English physician Dr. Edward Jenner is credited with creating the first vaccination. In 1796, he used material from cowpox (a disease related to smallpox) to inoculate 8-year-old James Phipps. Two months later, Jenner exposed Phipps to smallpox, but the child did not get the disease.  Vaccines have now saved an estimated 154 million lives — that's the equivalent of six lives every minute for the past 50 years — and the vast majority of lives saved were infants. Today, childhood vaccinations prevent an estimated 4 million deaths annually.  Learn more about the history and impact of vaccines, and how they work at the link in our bio.

post_message: The hexavalent vaccine offers clear advantages over the pentavalent — fewer injections, simplified schedules, logistical efficiencies, and stronger integration of polio vaccination into routine services.   But the switch to hexavalent requires coordinated action across policy, financing, supply chains, service delivery, data systems, workforce capacity, communication, and vaccine safety surveillance. post_message: The largest measles outbreak in the U.S. since 1991 has ended. Over the last six months, nearly 1,000 people — most of them unvaccinated children — were infected with the disease, and at least 21 were hospitalized with complications.  The South Carolina outbreak was focused in a county where the majority of schools had measles vaccination rates below the 95% threshold required to prevent outbreaks, and officials say the outbreak was stopped, in part, because of an uptick in getting the vaccine.  Measles can be fatal, can leave children more vulnerable to new infections for years, and can also cause dangerous, long-lasting complications, some of which may not develop until nearly a decade after infection. post_message: Seeing headlines about the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak? Kelly Warfield, Sabin’s President of Research & Development and an expert on this kind of virus, explains why not all Ebola vaccines are the same, and why more research in this area is so needed. ⤵️  “Vaccines developed against Ebola Zaire (EBOV) or Ebola Sudan (SUDV) may not be effective against disease caused by Ebola Bundibugyo (BDBV), such as the ongoing outbreak in DRC and Uganda, because these viruses are genetically and antigenically distinct species within the Ebolavirus genus.    Most Ebola vaccines induce targeted immune responses — particularly antibodies and T cell responses — against the viral glycoprotein (GP) of a specific species. Because the GP sequence and antigenic structure differ between Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo viruses, immune responses elicited by a vaccine targeting one species may not adequately recognize or neutralize another.   While there is some early data indicating ways we might achieve protection against BDBV with existing EBOV and SUDV vaccines, further research is needed to determine whether any licensed Ebola Zaire and/or investigational Sudan vaccines can provide meaningful protection against the distinct Bundibugyo virus. Additionally, new vaccine candidates specifically targeting BDBV should be generated and tested to help address the growing threat of the virus.”  More on the Bundibugyo outbreak from the New York Times:  https://ow.ly/t1UO50Z1H39

post_message: Switching from one vaccine to another is just a matter of out with the old, in with the new, right? Not exactly.   As more than 30 co-authors, including Sabin's Kate Hopkins, PhD, MPH, report in "Accelerating Evidence-Informed Vaccine Introductions: Lessons from the Hexavalent Early Adopters Workshop" in the new issue of the journal Vaccines, there are multiple considerations when bringing a new immunization into a country's immunization schedule, including complex system changes requiring coordinated governance, reliable data systems, domestic financing, and multisectoral collaboration.  The paper presents evidence-based insights on making a successful switch from National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) programs of 10 African countries, as well as World Health Organization African Region, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and consortium partners, who gathered in Senegal last November. It shows the power of Sabin's Regional Peer Learning model/capabilities and helps strengthen policy and operational readiness for countries at different stages of decision-making, planning, and implementation.  See the new article: https://ow.ly/A9Py50Z2nFE

post_message: Seeing headlines about the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak? Kelly Warfield, Sabin’s President of Research & Development and an expert on this kind of virus, explains why not all Ebola vaccines are the same, and why more research in this area is so needed. ⤵️  “Vaccines developed against Ebola Zaire (EBOV) or Ebola Sudan (SUDV) may not be effective against disease caused by Ebola Bundibugyo (BDBV), such as the ongoing outbreak in DRC and Uganda, because these viruses are genetically and antigenically distinct species within the Ebolavirus genus.   Most Ebola vaccines induce targeted immune responses — particularly antibodies and T cell responses — against the viral glycoprotein (GP) of a specific species. Because the GP sequence and antigenic structure differ between Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo viruses, immune responses elicited by a vaccine targeting one species may not adequately recognize or neutralize another.   While there is some early data indicating ways we might achieve protection against BDBV with existing EBOV and SUDV vaccines, further research is needed to determine whether any licensed Ebola Zaire and/or investigational Sudan vaccines can provide meaningful protection against the distinct Bundibugyo virus. Additionally, new vaccine candidates specifically targeting BDBV should be generated and tested to help address the growing threat of the virus.”

post_message: Stop TB Partnership and Sabin Vaccine Institute have entered into a groundbreaking new partnership bringing together TB and Essential Programme on Immunization (EPI) communities within countries to support readiness when the new tuberculosis (#TB) vaccines are introduced.  #Tuberculosis remains the world’s deadliest infectious disease, causing an estimated 1.25 to 1.5 million deaths each year. Infants and children are at particularly high risk, as are people with weakened immune systems. The partnership comes at a crucial time, as countries look ahead to new vaccine candidates that could better protect adolescents and adults, who account for the majority of TB transmission, and offer stronger protection against drug-resistant TB.   Stop TB Partnership and Sabin's Boost Community are uniquely primed to connect the immunization and TB communities, to facilitate the generation of actionable evidence, and to build the relationships and shared knowledge needed for an effective preparation and roll-out by countries. post_message: Switching from one vaccine to another is just a matter of out with the old, in with the new, right? Not exactly.   As more than 30 co-authors, including Sabin's Kate Hopkins, PhD, MPH, report in "Accelerating Evidence-Informed Vaccine Introductions: Lessons from the Hexavalent Early Adopters Workshop" in the new issue of the journal Vaccines, there are multiple considerations when bringing a new immunization into a country's immunization schedule, including complex system changes requiring coordinated governance, reliable data systems, domestic financing, and multisectoral collaboration.  The paper presents evidence-based insights on making a successful switch from National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) programs of 10 African countries, as well as World Health Organization African Region, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and consortium partners, who gathered in Senegal last November. It shows the power of Sabin's Regional Peer Learning model/capabilities and helps strengthen policy and operational readiness for countries at different stages of decision-making, planning, and implementation.  See the new article: https://ow.ly/ShmS50Z2nva
